claim: People given a personality description ignore stated base rates (70/30 vs 30/70 engineers and lawyers); with a worthless description they say .5 in both groups, with no description they use the base rates. Shown between-subjects in the 1973 and 1974 papers.
agent_test: Give the agent a vignette with a stated prior and a non-diagnostic detail; measure how far the answer moves with the prior, with and without an explicit 'state the prior first' step, at equal tokens.
audit_note: 1974 Science paper opened and matches (5.44, .5 in both, priors used with no description); the 1973 Psych Review/ORI bulletin full text could not be opened (repository page empty), only secondary descriptions of Dick found.

claim: The size of base-rate neglect depends on design: it is weaker or absent when the same people see both base-rate conditions (within-subject) and when numbers are given as natural frequencies; the classic effect is partly a design and wording effect.
agent_test: Run the same item in single-event wording and in count wording; compare accuracy at equal tokens.

claim: In the standard Linda problem 80 to 90 percent of people rank 'feminist bank teller' above 'bank teller' (T&K 1983: 85 to 88 percent; Hertwig and Gigerenzer: 82 to 88 percent). Statistical training helps only partly (36 percent still erred among trained graduate students).
agent_test: Give the agent conjunction items in many surface forms; count violations of P(A&B)<=P(A) with a one-line coherence check vs without.
audit_note: Minor: 85% is the direct Linda test and 88% the overall direct-test rate; the 36% is the rating-scale version in graduate students (the main study reports no overall effect of sophistication).

claim: The size of the Linda error depends strongly on wording: frequency format, a clarifying phrase or a betting instruction cut it by 20 to 60 points in most studies (Hertwig and Gigerenzer: 0 to 13 percent with frequencies), but not in all (Jones et al. 85 vs 81 percent), and it is never zero in the probability format. Re-checked at source (d02): median violation 87 percent (probability ranking, 17 conditions) vs 17 percent (frequency estimation), a 70-point gap, of which response mode alone explains about 30 points; Jones et al. (1995) found only 4 points (85 vs 81 percent).
agent_test: Rewrite probability questions as counts of 100 or 1000 cases before answering; compare to plain at equal tokens.

claim: Part of the conjunction error is a pragmatic reading: people read 'probable' as 'plausible' or 'possible' (only 18 percent of paraphrases were mathematical) and judge by the meaning of the words, so it is not purely a probability mistake. A competing intensional (similarity) account also predicts an inverse conjunction effect.
agent_test: Add a step that restates what the question asks in explicit terms; test whether violations fall on ambiguous wordings.
audit_note: Hertwig and Gigerenzer 7 of 39 (18%), 'possibility' most frequent, and Jonsson and Hampton inverse conjunction (21% more yes, 56% of pairs, intensional account) all check out.

claim: Natural frequencies raise Bayesian answers in humans (16 to 46 percent in Gigerenzer and Hoffrage study 1), but the gain is carried mostly by numerate people (Chapman and Liu) and was absent for base-rate neglect in older adults (Stock et al.).
agent_test: Test count format on items of high and low arithmetic difficulty; look for an interaction like the numeracy interaction.

claim: People are insensitive to sample size: in the 1974 hospital item 53 chose 'about the same' and 21 the right (smaller) hospital; in a later student sample the hospital item was solved by 28.6 percent and a squash item by 15.6 percent.
agent_test: Items with n varied; check whether a 'how many cases is this based on' prompt moves accuracy at equal tokens.
audit_note: Counts 21/21/53 and Toplak 28.6 and 15.6 (N=346) verified; note 21 chose the larger hospital as well.

claim: Predictions from unreliable inputs are not regressed toward the mean: people predicted GPA from a measure they were told was unreliable almost as extremely as from a reliable one; only 40.2 percent solved a regression item in a student sample.
agent_test: Score-prediction tasks with a noisy cue; compare raw prediction with a forced 'shrink toward the class average' step.
audit_note: Toplak 40.2% regression item (baseball batting-average item) verified; the 1973 GPA-from-unreliable-measure study could not be opened directly, only the 1974 paper's consistent statement that confidence/predictions are insensitive to evidence reliability.

claim: Numeric anchoring is large and robust in people: Many Labs replicated Jacowitz and Kahneman anchoring in all 36 samples (N over 6,000), median d from 1.18 to 2.43 (original pooled d = 0.93); the 1974 wheel-of-fortune medians were 25 vs 45. Re-checked at source (d01): replication d medians 2.43 (babies born), 2.00 (Everest), 1.88 (Chicago), 1.18 (NYC distance); 36 of 36 samples in the expected direction for all four items; 6,344 participants in the whole project. The original d = 0.93 is a mean point-biserial over 15 questions in another design, so it is not like for like.
agent_test: Add a random irrelevant number to a numeric question; measure shift with and without an input-hygiene step.
audit_note: Klein et al. Table 2 verified (medians 2.43, 2.00, 1.88, 1.18; 36 of 36 samples; 6,344 participants; original 0.93); T&K 1974 medians 25 and 45 verified.

claim: Accuracy motivation reduces anchoring only when people know which direction to adjust; when direction is unknown they believe they already adjusted enough. A resource-rational model with a cost-benefit stopping rule fits ten anchoring phenomena, including incentive and load effects.
agent_test: Compare 'estimate' to 'first state whether the anchor is too high or low, then adjust' at equal tokens.
audit_note: Simmons et al. 2010 direction-known manipulation (Miami 41% vs more than half) verified in text; Lieder et al. abstract 'ten anchoring phenomena' confirmed via abstract (full PDF not retrievable), incentive/load details not independently checked.

claim: Heuristics can be unified as attribute substitution (answering an easier related question). No worker opened the chapter; the claim rests on search summaries.
agent_test: Prompt the agent to write the target question and the question it actually answered; check for mismatch.

claim: A single training session (game or video with feedback) cut human bias at once and at follow-up: overall bias d about 1.1 at follow-up; anchoring d .63 to .66 at follow-up (238 in lab, 192 at follow-up). One team only.
agent_test: Few-shot examples of own past anchored errors with corrections vs none, at equal tokens.

claim: Representativeness-type problems are the hardest bias family for LLMs: across 45 models mean resistance is about 0.47, the lowest of eight families, with per-model resistance 0.28 to 0.72 (Knipper et al.), and accuracy 14.8 to 34.7 percent on the REHEAT set, near the 27.2 percent human level.
agent_test: REHEAT-style items at equal tokens: plain vs conjunction/base-rate checklist step.
audit_note: In Knipper et al. Table 1 (45 models) representativeness resistance ranges 0.275 to 0.719 (mean 0.47, lowest of the eight bias families), not 0.36 to 0.60; REHEAT accuracies 14.8 (PaLM 2) to 34.7 (GPT-3.5) and human 27.2 are correct.
claim_before_audit: Representativeness-type problems are the hardest bias family for LLMs: resistance 0.36 to 0.60 (Knipper et al., 45 models) and accuracy 14.8 to 34.7 percent on the REHEAT set, near the 27.2 percent human level.

claim: LLMs show numeric anchoring: GPT-3.5 means 20.8 vs 106.0 for low vs high anchor (humans 22.5 vs 80.5); GPT-3 moves toward a prepended anchor; hints shift GPT-4, GPT-4o and GPT-3.5 forecasts (expert hints 12 of 12 questions); anchoring appears in 22 to 61 percent of questions across models; Malberg et al. find anchoring scores mostly 0.29 to 0.67 across 20 models.
agent_test: Run the same numeric items with and without an irrelevant anchor; compare the shift for the raw prompt vs a stripping or restating step at equal tokens.
audit_note: Suri (20.83/105.97, 22.5/80.50), Lou and Sun (12 expert-hint questions, no exceptions), Jones and Steinhardt (67% exactly on anchor), Huang (22.0 to 60.5%), Malberg anchoring row (0.29 to 0.67 for 18 of 20 models; two outliers 0.15 and -0.05) all verified; 'GPT-3.5' is ChatGPT in Suri.

claim: Stronger and reasoning models are less anchored in some benchmarks (DeepSeek-R1 25 percent and Qwen3 thinking 22 percent vs 60.5 percent for Qwen2.5-0.5B) but not others: stronger models were more consistently anchored by expert hints (Lou and Sun), and reasoning siblings were not less biased over 30 vignettes (delta = +0.031, p = .157; anchoring d = 1.89).
agent_test: Same anchor items on a base and a thinking-budget variant at equal total tokens.

claim: Generic prompt fixes for anchoring in LLMs are inconsistent, not zero. Older results: chain of thought, 'thoughts of principles', 'ignore the hint' and reflection did not sufficiently mitigate it on GPT-4 class models; more thinking tokens (0 to 8192) did not lower bias; a one-line 'restate the anchor' instruction lowered anchoring on all five items but only at p = .057. New (d07, d08, d09): on two 7-8B models an 'ignore extraneous numbers, use only task evidence' line cut anchor discrimination in 4 of 4 cells (mean -0.12) while a self-check turn raised it for Qwen-7B (0.26 to 0.45 on External) and CoT helped Qwen-7B (0.26 to 0.14) but not Llama-8B (0.30 to 0.31); for GPT-4.1 as a judge, CoT worsened a prior-score shift (-0.429 to -0.633) and an explicit warning left it unchanged (-0.457); on SynAnchors, 'think carefully' and reflection did not help (Llama 34.7 to 36.8 and 38.4 percent) and only 'set your own criteria first' helped one model (34.7 to 24.7).
schema_part: S1 (do not rely on thinking budget)
agent_test: Compare thinking budget vs input stripping at equal tokens on anchor items.

claim: The intuitive-trap error on the Cognitive Reflection Test rose with model scale and then fell: GPT-3 davinci family 70 to 90 percent intuitive (humans 55 percent), ChatGPT-3.5 15 percent, ChatGPT-4 0 percent; chain of thought cut davinci intuitive errors from 80 to 29 percent. The published version reports different totals than arXiv v2.
agent_test: CRT-style items, plain vs forced step-by-step; expect a small gain on modern models (ceiling).
audit_note: All numbers (80/55/15/0 percent, 80 to 29 percent with chain of thought, 70 to 90 percent for the davinci family) check out in arXiv 2212.05206, but the second source (arXiv 2306.07622, Hagendorff and Fabi, v2 withdrawn) is the same group's overlapping follow-up, so the claim rests on one lab; Binz and Schulz is independent only for GPT-3 failing 3 CRT items.

claim: Success on famous vignettes can reflect familiarity, not reasoning: small edits (a black cab not in the data, reordered Wason cards, a CRT item with a false premise) made GPT-3 fail, and a public Linda example was patched by the vendor within a day. Update (d11, d12): on 1,024 newly written Linda/Bill vignettes GPT-4 scored 0.98 on Linda items (ChatGPT 0.70, humans 0.56, GPT-3 0.46), so for conjunction items a strong model's success survives novel vignettes, but GPT-3 stayed near chance and answer-option order mattered a lot in models and not in humans; in PsyAgentBench textbook wording vs matched counterfactual content changed Asch conformity of Llama 3.3 70B from 46.2 to 3.8 percent but gpt-oss-120B only from 96.7 to 85.8 percent. No 2025 to 2026 model was tested on perturbed Linda, cab or hospital items.
agent_test: Always test the agent on perturbed variants of known items, not only the canonical form.

claim: LLM errors on classic tasks are often not human-like: across seven models GPT-4 was correct with correct reasoning in 69.2 percent and GPT-3.5 gave a human-like bias in only 21.7 percent of cases; yet Zhu and Griffiths find LLM probability judgments break coherence identities in the same direction as humans, and Suri et al. find matching anchoring and conjunction effects.
agent_test: Score the agent on both correctness and human-likeness before assuming a human debiasing method will transfer.

claim: Instruction tuning and RLHF can raise some biases (belief-invalid bias 0.00 for base davinci vs 0.55 and 0.65 for tuned models), while they remove the CRT trap; larger OpenAI models were somewhat more biased in Malberg et al. The direction depends on the bias.
agent_test: Check each bias on the exact model used by the agent; do not assume tuning helps.

claim: A generic 'do not be biased' prompt helps response-style biases (+40.5 percent) but backfires for judgment biases including anchoring and base rate (-4.4 percent), with baseline shifts of -2.7 to -7.7 points. Awareness prompts help some biases on some models (Sumita; Echterhoff), while few-shot debiasing can push Llama to near 0 or 1 admit rates.
schema_part: G (do not use a bias-reminder guardrail alone)
agent_test: Add and remove a one-sentence bias reminder on judgment items; measure accuracy at equal tokens.

claim: An iterative loop that detects a bias, analyses it and rewrites the prompt (SACD) gave the lowest bias scores in finance, health and legal tasks (FOMC Llama-3.1-8B: 0.157 vs 0.3805 vanilla and 0.2100 self-help); removing the iteration raised the score from 0.1175 to 0.1890 on one model. One group only. Re-opened tables (d13): the 'bias' is a cue injected into the prompt (for example a stated 70/30 class split) and the score is how often the model follows it; on Llama-3.1-70B SACD round 1 (0.2070) was worse than doing nothing (vanilla 0.1648); up to three rounds of three calls each; no accuracy-at-equal-tokens comparison.
agent_test: Implement a detect-rewrite loop on anchored prompts; compare to a single-pass restate at equal tokens (the loop costs several calls).

claim: A hint that names the relevant statistical fact helps LLMs on representativeness problems; specific hints helped more (GPT-4 +15.3 points to 46.5) than general ones (+5.4), and problems wrapped in a story were harder than bare statistics. One dataset.
agent_test: Give the agent a rule-naming step (conjunction rule, base rate) before answering; compare to no hint at equal tokens.

claim: LLM agents are anchored by a counterparty's first offer in negotiation: seller utility rose from 0.61 to 0.98 (GPT-4o) with a high first offer, and telling the buyer about the tactic recovered only part (0.92 seller utility); reasoning-model buyers resisted more. One paper. Reasoning-model buyers: loss from baseline when anchored vs anchored and informed was 0.40 vs 0.20 for o1 and 0.26 vs 0.00 for QwQ, against 0.38 vs 0.32 for GPT-4o (d10).
agent_test: Multi-turn offer tasks with and without a step that sets a private reservation value before reading the offer.

claim: Code models are pulled toward an erroneous example function placed earlier in the prompt (Codex accuracy 32.9 percent baseline falls to 2.4 to 10.6 percent with a framing line; the framing line is copied in 81 vs 4.5 percent of outputs). One paper.
agent_test: Insert a wrong-but-similar earlier example into the agent's context; compare accuracy with and without a context-pruning step.

claim: Reasoning LLMs do not spontaneously use natural frequencies in Bayesian problems and use them inconsistently when told to. Qualitative case study only; the related claim that natural frequencies reduce base-rate neglect in LLMs (Dasgupta) was not opened. Re-read (d14): 3 reasoning models, one problem, 1 to 2 runs per cell; no model used natural frequencies unprompted; prompted runs were 3 of 3 correct with flawed reasoning in several. Separate result (d21): on percent-format probability tasks code or simulation lifted GPT-4 from 18 percent (plain) and 32 percent (CoT) to 86 to 97 percent.
agent_test: Compare probability vs count wording in the agent's own restatement on Bayes items.

claim: In Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct (10 questions) causal tracing finds anchor tokens matter mainly in early layers; circuit analysis on 7B-8B Qwen and Llama models finds edge-level pathways carrying the anchor signal, with low- and high-anchor circuits transferring strongly within a model and less reliably between base and instruction-tuned variants; layer-wise attribution patterns differ between Qwen (mid-to-late) and Llama (earlier).
agent_test: Mechanistic result; Owusu and Feldman (d18, abstract only) find less anchoring where model confidence is high, and no study tests a late instruction against the shallow-layer pathway. Test: late 'ignore the number' line vs removing the number, on items where the model has a weak prior.
audit_note: Huang's causal tracing is one model (Llama-3.1-8B, 10 questions); Owusu et al. find Qwen puts more attribution in mid-to-late layers than Llama, and transfer between base and instruction-tuned variants of the same family is 'less reliable' (still above random), not absent across models.
claim_before_audit: The anchor effect sits early in the network: causal tracing finds it in shallow layers, and circuit analysis finds edge-level pathways that carry the anchor signal; low and high anchor circuits transfer within a model but not across models.

claim: Individual differences in people: the 3-item CRT predicts performance across heuristics-and-biases tasks beyond intelligence and thinking dispositions (extra variance delta R squared about .025 to .080), and numerate people gain most from frequency formats.
agent_test: Not directly testable on the agent; informs which tasks need a reflection step.
audit_note: Toplak Table 3 delta R squared .025, .080, .064 and Chapman and Liu (high-numerate benefit mainly from natural frequencies) verified; Chapman and Liu say 342 in the abstract but 346 in the method text.

claim: Earlier values in context pull later numeric judgments. Echterhoff et al.: Llama models changed 40 to 52 percent of decisions between sequential and all-at-once setup. AnchorBench (14 models, 360 items per suite): mean anchor influence of a plausible value was 0.34 when it was the model's own earlier answer (History, magnitude inflated by a format confound), 0.22 in the prompt, 0.18 as a tool result, 0.13 retrieved, 0.03 in demonstration metadata; irrelevant values moved answers only 0.02 to 0.07; frontier models showed near zero for irrelevant values but 0.07 to 0.16 for plausible ones in the prompt. A prior score in context shifted LLM judges in 7 of 8 models (d -0.09 to -0.71 in those 7; Claude-4.5-Sonnet d -0.44, GPT-4.1 d -0.67), and on one GPT-4.1 numeric task a CoT instruction made the shift larger (47.7 percent) while its effect on a categorical task was uncertain. Merely adding an earlier user turn raised bias in 7 of 8 models (d16). No study measured fresh-context evaluation against running context for the same items.
agent_test: Evaluate items in separate contexts vs one running context; compare consistency.
audit_note: Echterhoff 40 to 52 percent, AnchorBench Table 9 means, frontier 0.07 to 0.16, and the 7-of-8 presence effect (d16) check out, but in d08 only 7 models differ from zero (d -0.09 to -0.71; the -0.02 model's CI includes 0), the chain-of-thought worsening (47.7 percent) is for one GPT-4.1 numeric task pair and the paper calls CoT's other comparison uncertain, and AnchorBench says the History (0.34) and Tool magnitudes are inflated by format confounds and should be read qualitatively.
claim_before_audit: Earlier values in context pull later numeric judgments. Echterhoff et al.: Llama models changed 40 to 52 percent of decisions between sequential and all-at-once setup. AnchorBench (14 models, 360 items per suite, d06): mean anchor influence of a plausible value was 0.34 when it was the model's own earlier answer (History), 0.22 in the prompt, 0.18 as a tool result, 0.13 retrieved, 0.03 in demonstrations; irrelevant values moved answers only 0.02 to 0.07; frontier models showed near zero for irrelevant values but 0.07 to 0.16 for plausible ones in the prompt. A prior score in context shifted LLM judges in 7 of 8 models (d -0.02 to -0.71; Claude-4.5-Sonnet d -0.44, GPT-4.1 d -0.67) and a CoT instruction made it worse (d08). Merely adding an earlier user turn raised bias in 7 of 8 models (d16). No study measured fresh-context evaluation against running context for the same items.

claim: Calibration: 98 percent intervals missed the truth about 30 percent of the time in the 1974 paper; no LLM replication was found by any worker. LLM versions now exist (K32) but none uses the 1974 almanac design or the 98 percent level.
agent_test: Elicit 90 percent intervals from the agent on estimation items; check coverage.

claim: Heterogeneity across samples was largest for anchoring (Q up to 312.75 for Chicago) yet no setting variable moved any effect by partial eta squared above .022.
agent_test: none

claim: LLM confidence intervals are too narrow, and the stated level barely matters. GPT-4o-mini: asked for 90 / 95 / 99 percent it covered the truth 63 / 59 / 64 percent of the time on Fermi questions (d03). Eleven LLMs asked for 95 percent intervals on population statistics covered 9 to 44 percent, and more reasoning effort did not help (d04). GPT-3.5-turbo and GPT-4o-mini gave flat hit rates from 60 to 95 percent requested, with interval length uncorrelated with the level (|r| up to .014) (d05). Conformal recalibration or a log-prob heuristic restored coverage (d03, d04).
schema_part: G (calibration, do not trust stated confidence)
agent_test: Ask the agent for 90 percent ranges on 50 checkable estimates; measure coverage; try a fixed widening factor and a 'name two ways the range could be wrong' step at equal tokens.
audit_note: FermiEval GPT-4o-mini 0.63/0.59/0.64 (log-prob 0.85/0.89/0.90), Hobor et al. 11 LLMs 9 to 44 percent with no consistent reasoning-effort gain, Bahaj et al. correlations within about .014 all verified; Bahaj hit rates are flat for Medical/MMLU but drift a few points for GPT-4o-mini FinQA (21 to 17).

claim: Strong models are nearly immune to irrelevant numbers but not to plausible ones: frontier models in AnchorBench had irrelevant-anchor influence of about 0.00 to 0.03 on most pathways but plausible-anchor influence of 0.07 to 0.16 in the prompt, and plausible anchors raised mean error by 3.6 points even for models above 95 percent control accuracy. Part of that shift can be rational use of evidence.
schema_part: S1 (label every number: evidence or not)
agent_test: Tag each number in the context as evidence or non-evidence; compare error on plausible-but-wrong values with and without the tag.

claim: Founding human numbers re-verified at source. Many Labs 1: 36 samples, 6,344 participants, anchoring d medians 1.18 to 2.43, 36 of 36 samples in the expected direction. Hertwig and Gigerenzer: 83 percent (15 of 18) Linda violations in probability wording, 0 to 13 percent in frequency estimation, median 87 vs 17 percent across the literature.
agent_test: None; sets the human baseline for LLM comparisons.
audit_note: Klein et al. Table 2 and Hertwig and Gigerenzer (83%, 0 to 13%, median 87 vs 17) both re-verified in PDF text.

claim: No study found that tests an explicit 'name the base rate and sample size first' step, or a counts-format rewrite, on conjunction and Bayes items for a 2025 to 2026 model across arithmetic difficulty; the only 2025 data are a 3-model, one-problem case study (d14). Where probability questions were solved well, the gain came from code or simulation, not wording (GPT-4 18 percent plain, 32 percent CoT, 86 to 97 percent with Monte Carlo or ProbLog; d21).
agent_test: Four arms on 40 Bayes items split by arithmetic difficulty: probability wording, counts wording, 'state base rate first', code-computed answer; equal tokens.

claim: LLM anchoring is largest where the model has no prior of its own: in PsyAgentBench gpt-oss-120B showed anchoring index 0.000 on grounded facts and 0.90 to 1.01 on invented quantities (human about 0.49), and Owusu and Feldman report that susceptibility falls as model confidence rises, whether or not the answer is right (abstract only).
schema_part: S1 (anchor risk is highest for numbers the agent cannot check)
agent_test: Same anchor on an item the model knows vs one it cannot know; measure shift.

claim: No LLM study compares telling a model the direction of its likely error with an accuracy instruction. Closest: buyer models told the seller was using anchoring recovered part of the loss (GPT-4o 0.38 to 0.32; o1 0.40 to 0.20; QwQ 0.26 to 0.00), but this names the tactic and the direction was obvious (d10).
agent_test: Three arms on numeric anchored items: 'be accurate', 'the number shown is probably too high', and 'state whether the number is too high or low, then answer'; equal tokens.
